name: Vitamin K eye cream

card.summary: Topical vitamin K is marketed for under-eye dark circles said to have a blood-vessel component; no clinical studies of it have been published.
card.aka: Phytonadione eye cream, vitamin K dark circle cream
card.note: No clinical studies exist; its effect on dark circles is unproven.

quick.overview:
Vitamin K eye cream is a cosmetic product applied under the eyes and marketed for dark circles with a vascular or bruise-like component. Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin best known for its role in blood clotting.
No clinical studies of topical vitamin K for dark circles have been published, so claims about its effect on under-eye darkness remain untested.
quick.mechanism: Vitamin K is a cofactor for an enzyme that modifies clotting proteins, which is how it supports blood coagulation. Proponents of the cream link that clotting role to reducing blood pooling under the eyes; this link has not been tested in studies found for this entry.
quick.risks: Reference material on vitamin K notes that no toxicity is known from high oral intakes of K1 or K2, while intravenous injection can cause severe reactions. Those findings concern oral and injected forms, not creams. Dark circles have many causes, including anatomy, pigmentation, allergies and thin skin.

lead: Vitamin K eye cream is a topical cosmetic product applied to the skin under the eyes and marketed to improve the look of dark circles, especially the bluish or purplish kind that people attribute to blood showing through thin skin. Users apply it as part of an eye-area routine, usually alongside sunscreen and moisturiser, aiming for a brighter, less tired-looking under-eye.

The ingredient is vitamin K, a family of fat-soluble vitamins that includes K1 (phylloquinone) from plants and K2 (menaquinones) from animal and fermented foods. In the body it acts as a cofactor for the enzyme that activates clotting proteins [1]. Brands extend that clotting role to the skin, proposing that it may help with pooled blood and bruise-like discolouration, and many sell it combined with retinol, caffeine or vitamin C.

Research on topical vitamin K is concentrated on bruising after pulsed dye laser treatment, where small split-face trials have reported mixed results [5][7][8], and on bruising after eyelid surgery, which an American Academy of Ophthalmology review covered [4]. Studies of vitamin K specifically for under-eye dark circles are limited to a small single-blind trial of a caffeine and vitamin K pad [9].

chain: Marketed to reduce blood pooling and bruise-like colour
Under-eye area looks brighter and less shadowed
angle.text: People apply vitamin K cream to the lower eyelid area hoping to lighten bluish or purplish dark circles and make the eyes look more rested. Brands pair it with moisturising and brightening ingredients that can also contribute to a smoother-looking under-eye.

paras: Wikipedia's article on periorbital dark circles lists many contributors: bone structure and a prominent orbicularis oculi muscle, very thin eyelid skin, allergy and eye rubbing, medications that dilate vessels, iron or B12 deficiency, sleep loss, ageing with collagen loss, sun-driven pigmentation and increased melanin around the eyes [2].

The same article groups causes by mechanism: vascular (visible blood flow), pigmentary (melanin), structural (anatomy and ageing) and systemic (allergy, anaemia, cortisol, medication). It names caffeine as a vasoconstrictor said to improve the look of dark circles, vitamin C for brightening pigmentation, and procedures such as lasers, intense pulsed light, fat transplantation and hyaluronic acid fillers [2]. It does not discuss vitamin K. Reviews of eye-contour products note that most evidence comes from multi-ingredient formulas, with short, often industry-sponsored studies [10].

sections.h: Vitamin K in the body and on the skin
paras: Vitamin K is needed for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase to modify clotting factors so they can bind calcium; deficiency impairs coagulation [1]. Cosmetic brands build on this role, and commonly say that topical vitamin K may support vessel integrity and help the skin clear small leaks of blood, which is the reasoning behind its use on bruising and under-eye discolouration.

A 2026 review in Clinics in Dermatology describes vitamin K as having roles beyond coagulation and reports that topical vitamin K has been studied for wound healing, resolution of purpura after laser treatment and prevention of cetuximab-induced dermatitis [3]. Product pages from skincare brands present vitamin K as one ingredient in a multi-active eye formula, and some state that their own testing shows reduced dark circles or puffiness; these are company claims.

Danish scientist Henrik Dam identified a bleeding-related factor in chicks in 1929 and called it the coagulation vitamin; the letter K comes from the German Koagulationsvitamin. Dam and Edward Doisy, who worked out its structure, shared the 1943 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine [1]. Vitamin K1 is found in leafy greens, while K2 forms such as MK-7 are found in animal foods and in natto [1].

Eye creams are applied in small amounts with a fingertip to the orbital bone area, usually morning and evening. Vitamin K products are often chosen by people whose dark circles look blue-purple or worsen when tired, rather than brown, since brown shadowing is generally associated with pigmentation [2]. Concealer, sunscreen and sleep are common companions in the same routine. Many formulas combine vitamin K with retinol, caffeine, vitamin C or peptides; a 2026 review of periocular dermocosmetics lists retinoids, peptides, antioxidants, vasomodulators and depigmenting agents as the classes studied for the eye area [10].

Laser bruising studies are the main body of human data on topical vitamin K. In a 1999 prospective study of 20 adults, a cream with 1 percent vitamin K and 0.3 percent retinol applied for two weeks before and after pulsed dye laser resolved purpura faster than no application, with significance from day 3 onward [8]. A 2002 double-blind split-face study of 22 patients found that two weeks of vitamin K cream after laser treatment significantly reduced bruising severity compared with placebo, while pretreatment alone did not [7]. A 2009 split-face trial of a vitamin K oxide gel in 20 patients reported more consistent purpura resolution on the active side from day 2, but the differences were not statistically significant over the 9-day study [5]. A 2004 letter in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology was titled as finding no effect of topical vitamin K on bruising after mechanical injury [6].

The American Academy of Ophthalmology reviewed 11 studies of homeopathic agents and vitamins for bruising after oculofacial surgery. It reported that in two studies vitamin K cream was equivalent to placebo, and concluded that the literature did not support using these agents to reduce ecchymosis after oculofacial or pulsed dye laser surgery; no serious side effects were identified [4].

For dark circles, a 2015 single-blind study applied a pad containing 3 percent caffeine and 1 percent vitamin K in an emu-oil emulsion under one eye and a water pad under the other in 11 women for four weeks. The authors reported reduced dark circles and wrinkle depth on the active side in all participants, using visual assessment and a skin-analysis instrument; the report does not give statistical tests and the sample was small [9]. Other dark-circle trials have tested multi-active serums that did not contain vitamin K, such as a 2025 study of a niacinamide, arbutin and tranexamic acid formula that reported a 47.9 percent average reduction in under-eye hyperpigmentation [11].

Reference text notes that no toxicity is known from high oral intakes of vitamin K1 or K2, while intravenous K1 can rarely cause severe reactions, and people on warfarin are advised to keep vitamin K intake consistent [1]. The 2026 dermatology review adds that systemic vitamin K, notably intramuscular injection, has been linked to skin reactions such as eczematous plaques [3]. These statements concern oral and injected vitamin K; cosmetic creams are applied in small amounts to skin, and the laser-bruising trials reported no treatment-related adverse effects [5]. As with any eye-area product, labels advise avoiding contact with the eyes and stopping use if irritation appears.

timeline.event: Henrik Dam reports a coagulation factor in chicks, later named vitamin K [1].
Dam and Edward Doisy share the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on vitamin K [1].
A study of topical vitamin K plus retinol on laser-induced purpura is published in Dermatologic Surgery [8].
A split-face trial reports that post-laser vitamin K cream reduced bruising [7].
A letter in JAAD reports no effect of topical vitamin K on bruising after mechanical injury [6].
A split-face trial of vitamin K oxide gel after pulsed dye laser reports faster purpura resolution that is not statistically significant [5].
A small single-blind study tests a caffeine and vitamin K eye pad for dark circles [9].
The American Academy of Ophthalmology reviews bruising remedies after oculofacial surgery, including vitamin K cream [4].
A review in Clinics in Dermatology summarises topical vitamin K uses [3].

lore.intro: Vitamin K eye cream is discussed in skincare circles as a product for blue-purple dark circles, often as part of a multi-ingredient eye cream.

claims.claim: Vitamin K helps vascular, bluish dark circles.
claims.believers: Brands and users say its clotting role helps with blood pooling and bruise-like colour under the eyes, and that it works best on bluish circles.
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes vascular circles as dilated vessels showing through thin skin and does not discuss vitamin K [2]; a single-blind study of 11 women of a caffeine and vitamin K pad reported reduced dark circles [9].

claims.believers: Users apply it after cosmetic procedures expecting faster fading of bruises.
claims.experts: Two small laser trials reported faster purpura resolution with vitamin K products, one trial did not reach significance, and the AAO review of oculofacial surgery studies found vitamin K cream equivalent to placebo [4][5][7][8].

claims.claim: Pairing it with retinol or caffeine improves results.
claims.believers: Brands combine vitamin K with retinol, caffeine and vitamin C in single products.
claims.experts: The 1999 study used vitamin K with retinol [8] and the 2015 pad study used vitamin K with caffeine [9]; reviewers note most eye-area evidence comes from multi-ingredient formulas [10].

claims.claim: Brown dark circles will not respond to vitamin K.
claims.believers: Users say vitamin K targets bluish circles while pigmented brown circles need brighteners.
claims.experts: Wikipedia associates brown shadowing with pigmentation, for which vitamin C and other agents are discussed [2].

claims.claim: Topical vitamin K is safe because the vitamin is non-toxic.
claims.believers: Brands point to the vitamin's established safety in food and supplements.
claims.experts: Known non-toxicity applies to oral intake, while intravenous and intramuscular vitamin K have caused reactions [1][3]; creams were not associated with adverse effects in the laser trials [5].
